api: API available on higher tiers for transcript retrieval and workflow integration.
cons: Recording consent exposure is serious and jurisdiction-dependent
Speaker attribution errors carry real consequences
name: Otter.ai
pros: Strong searchable archive across many meetings
files: Live meeting audio plus uploaded audio and video files.
value: Joins meetings, transcribes them, and produces searchable notes and summaries automatically. Removes note-taking overhead entirely, which is why adoption tends to spread through an organization without anyone approving it.
engine: Proprietary speech recognition and summarisation models.
latency: Real-time captioning during the meeting; summaries follow shortly after.
quality: Strong on clear audio and standard accents. Degrades with crosstalk, heavy accents, and specialised vocabulary, and summaries occasionally attribute a statement to the wrong speaker, which matters more than a plain transcription error.
tagline: Meeting transcription and notes, and the tool most likely to create a consent problem.
use_cases: Automatic transcripts and summaries of recurring internal meetings
Searchable archive of decisions across many calls
Accessibility, live captioning for participants who need it
governance_note: The highest-risk tool in ordinary daily use, and the risk is legal rather than technical. Recording consent law varies by jurisdiction: several US states require all-party consent, and recording a call without it is a criminal matter in some of them, not a policy breach. Add legal privilege, HR investigations, and regulated client conversations and the exposure compounds. Any deployment needs an explicit consent practice, a retention policy, and a clear list of meeting types where it must never join. This is also the tool most often found in an AI inventory that nobody approved.
training_optout: Business and enterprise tiers offer data controls. Consumer tiers differ. Verify before any privileged or regulated conversation is recorded.
